chapters.title: Story of the Door
paragraphs: Mr. Utterson the lawyer had a rugged face that no smile ever lit. He was cold, sparing and awkward in conversation, slow to show feeling, lean, tall, dusty and dreary, and yet somehow lovable. At friendly gatherings, when the wine was to his liking, something deeply human shone in his eye. It never found its way into his talk, but it spoke not only through these silent signs on his after-dinner face, but more often and more loudly in the actions of his life. He was strict with himself. He drank gin when he was alone, to punish his taste for fine vintages, and though he enjoyed the theatre, he had not set foot in one for twenty years. Toward others, however, he had a well-proven tolerance. He sometimes wondered, almost with envy, at the sheer force of spirits that went into their misdeeds, and in any extremity he was more inclined to help than to reprove. “I incline to Cain’s heresy,” he used to say, in his odd way. “I let my brother go to the devil in his own fashion.” Being such a man, he often found himself the last respectable acquaintance and the last good influence in the lives of people on the downward road. And to these, as long as they came to his chambers, he never showed the slightest change of manner.

No doubt this was easy for Mr. Utterson, since he was undemonstrative at the best of times, and even his friendships seemed to rest on the same broad good nature. A modest man accepts his circle of friends ready-made from the hands of chance, and that was the lawyer’s way. His friends were his own relatives or the people he had known longest. His affections grew with time, like ivy, and did not depend on any fitness in the person loved. Hence, no doubt, the bond between him and Mr. Richard Enfield, his distant kinsman and a well-known man about town. Many people found it a puzzle what these two could see in each other, or what they could find to talk about. Those who met them on their Sunday walks said that they spoke not a word, looked remarkably dull, and greeted the arrival of a friend with obvious relief. All the same, the two men valued these outings above everything, counted them the finest jewel of each week, and not only put aside chances of pleasure but even held out against the calls of business so that they could enjoy them without interruption.

On one of these rambles it happened that their way took them down a side street in a busy part of London. The street was small and what is called quiet, but on weekdays it did a thriving trade. Its inhabitants all seemed to be doing well, and all competed in hoping to do better still, spending what they had left over from their profits on finery. The shop fronts stood along the street with an inviting air, like rows of smiling saleswomen. Even on Sunday, when it hid its showier charms and lay fairly empty of traffic, the street shone out against its shabby surroundings like a fire in a forest. With its freshly painted shutters, well-polished brasses, and general cleanliness and cheerful note, it caught the eye of the passer-by at once and pleased it.

Two doors from one corner, on the left going east, the line of shops was broken by the opening of a court. Just there, a sinister block of building pushed its gable forward over the street. It was two storeys high and showed no window, only a door on the lower storey and a blind forehead of discoloured wall above. Every feature bore the marks of long and squalid neglect. The door had neither bell nor knocker, and its paint was blistered and stained. Tramps slouched into the recess and struck matches on the panels, children played shop on the steps, and a schoolboy had tried his knife on the mouldings. For close on a generation no one had come to drive off these casual visitors or to repair the damage they did.
Mr. Enfield and the lawyer were walking on the far side of the street, but when they drew level with the entry, Enfield lifted his cane and pointed.
“Have you ever noticed that door?” he asked. When his companion said he had, he added, “In my mind it is linked with a very odd story.”
“Is it?” said Mr. Utterson, his voice changing slightly. “And what was the story?”

“Well, this is how it was,” Mr. Enfield answered. “I was coming home from some place at the end of the world, at about three o’clock on a black winter morning. My way led through a part of town where there was literally nothing to see but lamps. Street after street, with everyone asleep—street after street, all lit up as if for a procession and all as empty as a church—until at last I got into the state of mind where a man listens and listens and starts to long for the sight of a policeman. All at once I saw two figures. One was a little man stumping along eastward at a good pace, and the other was a girl of maybe eight or ten, running as hard as she could down a cross street. Well, sir, the two ran into each other at the corner, naturally enough. And then came the horrible part of it, for the man calmly trampled over the child’s body and left her screaming on the ground. It sounds like nothing to hear, but it was hellish to see. It wasn’t like a man. It was like some damned Juggernaut. I let out a few halloas, took to my heels, grabbed my gentleman by the collar, and brought him back to where quite a group had already gathered around the screaming child. He was perfectly cool and put up no resistance, but he gave me one look, so ugly that it brought the sweat out on me as if I’d been running. The people who had turned out were the girl’s own family, and soon the doctor arrived, the one she had been sent for. Well, the child was not much the worse—more frightened than hurt, according to the Sawbones—and you might have supposed that would be the end of it. But there was one curious circumstance. I had taken a loathing to my gentleman at first sight. So had the child’s family, which was only natural. But it was the doctor who struck me. He was the usual cut-and-dried apothecary, of no particular age or colour, with a strong Edinburgh accent and about as emotional as a bagpipe. Well, sir, he was like the rest of us. Every time he looked at my prisoner, I saw that Sawbones turn sick and white with the wish to kill him. I knew what was in his mind, just as he knew what was in mine. Since killing was out of the question, we did the next best thing. We told the man we could and would make such a scandal of this that his name would stink from one end of London to the other. If he had any friends or any credit, we promised him he would lose them. And all the time, as we were piling it on red hot, we were keeping the women off him as well as we could, for they were as wild as harpies. I never saw such a circle of hateful faces. And there was the man in the middle, with a kind of black, sneering coolness—frightened too, I could see that—but carrying it off, sir, really like Satan. ‘If you choose to make capital out of this accident,’ said he, ‘I am naturally helpless. No gentleman wants a scene,’ says he. ‘Name your figure.’ Well, we screwed him up to a hundred pounds for the child’s family. He clearly would have liked to hold out, but there was something about the lot of us that meant mischief, and at last he gave in. The next thing was to get the money, and where do you think he took us but to that place with the door? He whipped out a key, went in, and soon came back with ten pounds or so in gold and a cheque for the rest, on Coutts’s, made payable to bearer and signed with a name I can’t mention, though it is one of the points of my story. It was a name, at least, that is very well known and often printed. The sum was steep, but the signature was good for more than that, if it was genuine. I took the liberty of pointing out to my gentleman that the whole business looked suspect, and that in real life a man doesn’t walk into a cellar door at four in the morning and come out with another man’s cheque for close on a hundred pounds. But he was quite easy and sneering. ‘Set your mind at rest,’ says he. ‘I will stay with you until the banks open and cash the cheque myself.’ So off we all went—the doctor, the child’s father, our friend and myself—and we spent the rest of the night in my chambers. Next day, when we had breakfasted, we went in a body to the bank. I handed in the cheque myself and said I had every reason to believe it was a forgery. Not a bit of it. The cheque was genuine.”
“Tut-tut!” said Mr. Utterson.

“I see you feel as I do,” said Mr. Enfield. “Yes, it’s a bad story. My man was a fellow nobody could have anything to do with, a really damnable man. And the person who drew the cheque is the very pink of respectability, famous too, and—what makes it worse—one of those fellows who do what they call good. Blackmail, I suppose: an honest man paying through the nose for some prank of his youth. So I call the place with the door Black Mail House. Though even that, you know, is far from explaining everything,” he added, and with those words he fell into a musing mood.
Mr. Utterson brought him out of it by asking rather suddenly, “And you don’t know whether the man who drew the cheque lives there?”
“Likely enough, isn’t it?” Mr. Enfield answered. “But I happen to have noticed where he lives. It’s in some square or other.”
“And you never inquired about the—place with the door?” asked Mr. Utterson.

“No, sir. I felt some delicacy,” was the answer. “I feel strongly about asking questions. It has too much of the day of judgment about it. You ask one question, and it’s like setting a stone rolling. You’re sitting quietly at the top of a hill, and off goes the stone, knocking others loose. Before long some mild old gentleman, the last person you’d have expected, is struck down in his own back garden, and his family must change their name. No, sir, I have a rule: the more a business looks like Queer Street, the fewer questions I ask.”
“A very good rule, too,” said the lawyer.

“But I’ve studied the place for myself,” Mr. Enfield went on. “It scarcely looks like a house. There is no other door, and no one goes in or out of this one except, very rarely, the gentleman of my adventure. On the first floor, three windows face the court, and there are none below. The windows are always shut, but they’re clean. There’s also a chimney, which is usually smoking, so someone must live there. Yet even that isn’t certain, because the buildings crowd so close around the court that it’s hard to tell where one stops and the next begins.”
The pair walked on in silence for a while. Then Mr. Utterson said, “Enfield, that’s a good rule of yours.”
“Yes, I think it is,” Enfield replied.
“Even so,” the lawyer pressed on, “there is one thing I want to ask you. What was the name of the man who walked over the child?”
“Well,” said Mr. Enfield, “I can’t see the harm in it. The man’s name was Hyde.”
“Hm,” said Mr. Utterson. “And what does he look like?”

“That isn’t easy to say. Something is wrong with the way he looks—something unpleasant, something plainly detestable. I never disliked a man so much, and yet I can hardly tell you why. He must be deformed somewhere. He gives a strong impression of deformity, though I couldn’t put my finger on the place. He looks extraordinary, and yet when I try, I can name nothing out of the ordinary. No, sir, I can’t make anything of it. I can’t describe him. And it isn’t that I forget, for I swear I can see him at this moment.”
Mr. Utterson walked on again for some way in silence, plainly weighed down by thought. “You are sure he used a key?” he asked at last.
“My dear sir…” began Enfield, startled out of himself.

“Yes, I know,” said Utterson. “I know it must seem odd to you. The truth is, I haven’t asked you the other man’s name because I know it already. Your story has hit home, you see, Richard. If you got any detail wrong, you had better put it right.”

“You might have warned me,” returned the other, a little sullenly. “But I have been exact to the point of pedantry, as you put it. The fellow had a key, and what’s more, he has it still. Not a week ago I saw him use it.”

Mr. Utterson gave a deep sigh but said nothing, and after a moment the young man continued. “That teaches me to hold my tongue once more,” he said. “I’m ashamed of how long mine is. Let’s agree never to speak of this again.”
“Gladly,” said the lawyer. “Here’s my hand on it, Richard.”

chapters.title: Search for Mr. Hyde
paragraphs: That evening Mr. Utterson came home to his bachelor house in a sombre mood and sat down to dinner without relish. On Sundays it was his habit, once the meal was over, to sit close by the fire with some volume of dry divinity on his reading desk, until the clock of the neighbouring church struck twelve, when he would go soberly and gratefully to bed. This night, however, as soon as the cloth was taken away, he picked up a candle and went into his business room. There he opened his safe, took from its most private corner a document marked on the envelope as Dr. Jekyll’s Will, and sat down with a clouded brow to study it. The will was in Jekyll’s own handwriting, for Mr. Utterson, though he had taken charge of it now that it was made, had refused to give the least help in drawing it up. It provided that if Henry Jekyll, M.D., D.C.L., L.L.D., F.R.S., etc., should die, all his possessions were to pass into the hands of his “friend and benefactor Edward Hyde.” It also provided that if Dr. Jekyll should “disappear or be absent without explanation for any period exceeding three calendar months,” the said Edward Hyde was to step into the said Henry Jekyll’s shoes without further delay, free of any burden or obligation beyond paying a few small sums to the members of the doctor’s household. This document had long been an eyesore to the lawyer. It offended him both as a lawyer and as a lover of the sane and customary side of life, to whom anything fanciful was immodest. Until now it was his ignorance of Mr. Hyde that had swelled his indignation. Now, by a sudden turn, it was his knowledge. It had been bad enough when the name was only a name, and he could learn no more of it. It was worse when the name began to be clothed in detestable attributes. Out of the shifting, insubstantial mists that had so long baffled his eye, there leaped up the sudden, definite image of a fiend.
“I took it for madness,” he said, putting the objectionable paper back in the safe, “and now I begin to fear it is disgrace.”

With that he blew out his candle, put on a greatcoat, and set off toward Cavendish Square, that citadel of medicine, where his friend the great Dr. Lanyon had his house and saw his crowds of patients. “If anyone knows, it will be Lanyon,” he had thought.

The solemn butler knew him and welcomed him. There was no waiting for him. He was shown straight from the door into the dining-room, where Dr. Lanyon sat alone over his wine. Lanyon was a hearty, healthy, dapper, red-faced gentleman with a shock of prematurely white hair and a loud, decided manner. At the sight of Mr. Utterson he sprang up from his chair and welcomed him with both hands. His warmth, as was usual with him, looked rather theatrical, but it rested on genuine feeling. These two were old friends, old schoolmates and college mates, who thoroughly respected themselves and each other and—which does not always follow—thoroughly enjoyed each other’s company.
After some rambling talk, the lawyer led round to the subject that so disagreeably occupied his mind.
“I suppose, Lanyon,” he said, “that you and I must be the two oldest friends Henry Jekyll has?”
“I wish they were younger friends,” chuckled Dr. Lanyon. “But I suppose we are. What of it? I hardly see him these days.”
“Do you?” said Utterson. “I thought you had a common interest.”

“We had,” was the reply. “But it is more than ten years since Henry Jekyll became too fanciful for me. He began to go wrong, wrong in his mind. Of course I still take an interest in him for old times’ sake, as they say, but I see devilish little of him, and I have for years. Such unscientific balderdash,” added the doctor, flushing suddenly purple, “would have estranged Damon and Pythias.”

This small burst of temper came as something of a relief to Mr. Utterson. “They have only differed over some point of science,” he thought. Being a man with no scientific passions (except in the matter of conveyancing), he even added, “It is nothing worse than that!” He gave his friend a few seconds to regain his composure, and then came to the question he had come to ask. “Did you ever come across a _protégé_ of his—a man called Hyde?” he asked.
“Hyde?” repeated Lanyon. “No. Never heard of him. He must be since my time.”

That was all the information the lawyer took home with him to the great, dark bed where he tossed and turned until the small hours of the morning began to grow large. It was a night of little ease for his toiling mind, which toiled in pure darkness and was besieged by questions.

Six o’clock struck on the bells of the church that stood so conveniently near Mr. Utterson’s house, and still he was digging at the problem. Until now it had touched him only on the intellectual side, but now his imagination was engaged too, or rather enslaved. As he lay tossing in the heavy darkness of the night and the curtained room, Mr. Enfield’s tale passed before his mind like a scroll of lighted pictures. He would be aware of the great field of lamps of a city at night, then of the figure of a man walking quickly, then of a child running from the doctor’s, and then the two met, and that human Juggernaut trod the child down and passed on, heedless of her screams. Or else he would see a room in a rich house where his friend lay asleep, dreaming and smiling at his dreams. Then the door of that room would open, the curtains of the bed be pulled apart, the sleeper be called back, and—look!—there would stand at his side a figure to whom power was given, and even at that dead hour he must get up and do its bidding. This figure, in these two phases, haunted the lawyer all night. If he dozed at any moment, it was only to see it glide more stealthily through sleeping houses, or move faster and still faster, even to dizziness, through wider labyrinths of lamplit city, and at every street corner crush a child and leave her screaming. And still the figure had no face by which he might know it. Even in his dreams it had no face, or one that baffled him and melted before his eyes. And so there sprang up and quickly grew in the lawyer’s mind a singularly strong, almost excessive, curiosity to see the features of the real Mr. Hyde. If he could only once set eyes on him, he thought, the mystery would lighten and perhaps roll away altogether, as mysterious things tend to do when they are well examined. He might see a reason for his friend’s strange preference or bondage (call it which you please) and even for the startling clauses of the will. At least it would be a face worth seeing: the face of a man without a trace of mercy, a face that had only to show itself to rouse a spirit of lasting hatred in the unimpressionable Enfield.

From that time on, Mr. Utterson began to haunt the door in the side street of shops. He could be found at his chosen post in the morning before office hours, at noon when business was brisk and time scarce, and at night under the face of the foggy city moon—in all lights and at all hours, whether the street was lonely or crowded.
“If he is Mr. Hyde,” he had thought, “then I shall be Mr. Seek.”

And at last his patience was rewarded. It was a fine dry night with frost in the air. The streets were as clean as a ballroom floor, and the lamps, undisturbed by any wind, drew a regular pattern of light and shadow. By ten o’clock, when the shops were closed, the side street was very solitary and, despite the low growl of London from all around, very silent. Small sounds carried far. Household noises from the houses could be heard clearly on either side of the roadway, and the sound of any passer-by’s approach reached the ear long before he did. Mr. Utterson had been at his post for some minutes when he became aware of an odd, light footstep coming near. In the course of his nightly patrols he had long grown used to the curious way the footfalls of a single person, while he is still far off, suddenly stand out distinct from the vast hum and clatter of the city. Yet his attention had never before been so sharply and decisively caught, and it was with a strong, superstitious foreknowledge of success that he withdrew into the entry of the court.

The steps drew rapidly nearer and suddenly swelled louder as they turned the end of the street. Looking out from the entry, the lawyer could soon see what kind of man he had to deal with. He was small and very plainly dressed, and the look of him, even at that distance, somehow went strongly against the watcher’s inclination. But he made straight for the door, crossing the roadway to save time, and as he came he drew a key from his pocket like a man approaching home.
Mr. Utterson stepped forward and tapped him on the shoulder as he went by. “Mr. Hyde, I believe?”

Mr. Hyde shrank back, drawing his breath in with a hiss. But his fear lasted only a moment, and though he did not look the lawyer in the face, he answered coolly enough, “That is my name. What do you want?”

“I see you are going in,” the lawyer replied. “I am an old friend of Dr. Jekyll’s—Mr. Utterson of Gaunt Street—you must have heard my name. Meeting you so conveniently, I thought you might let me in.”
“You will not find Dr. Jekyll. He is from home,” replied Mr. Hyde, blowing into the key. And then, suddenly but still without looking up, he asked, “How did you know me?”
“In return,” said Mr. Utterson, “will you do me a favour?”
“With pleasure,” replied the other. “What is it?”
“Will you let me see your face?” asked the lawyer.

Mr. Hyde seemed to hesitate. Then, as if on some sudden thought, he turned to face him with an air of defiance, and the pair stared at each other quite fixedly for a few seconds. “Now I shall know you again,” said Mr. Utterson. “It may be useful.”
“Yes,” returned Mr. Hyde, “it is as well that we have met. And _by the way_, you should have my address.” And he gave the number of a street in Soho.
“Good God!” thought Mr. Utterson. “Can he, too, have been thinking of the will?” But he kept his feelings to himself and only grunted to acknowledge the address.
“And now,” said the other, “how did you know me?”
“From a description,” was the reply.
“Whose description?”
“We have friends in common,” said Mr. Utterson.
“Friends in common,” echoed Mr. Hyde, a little hoarsely. “Who are they?”
“Jekyll, for instance,” said the lawyer.
“He never told you that,” cried Mr. Hyde, flushing with anger. “I didn’t think you would tell a lie.”
“Come now,” said Mr. Utterson, “that is not the way to speak.”
The other broke into a savage, snarling laugh. In the next moment, moving with extraordinary speed, he had unlocked the door and vanished into the house.

When Mr. Hyde had left him, the lawyer stood a while, the picture of disquiet. Then he began to climb the street slowly, pausing every step or two and putting his hand to his brow like a man in mental perplexity. The problem he was debating as he walked is of a kind that is rarely solved. Mr. Hyde was pale and dwarfish. He gave an impression of deformity without any nameable malformation. He had a displeasing smile, he had behaved toward the lawyer with a sort of murderous mixture of timidity and boldness, and he spoke in a husky, whispering and somewhat broken voice. All these were points against him, but not all of them together could explain the disgust, loathing and fear, new to him, with which Mr. Utterson regarded him. “There must be something else,” said the perplexed gentleman. “There _is_ something more, if I could only find a name for it. God bless me, the man hardly seems human! Something troglodytic, shall we say? Or can it be the old story of Dr. Fell? Or is it just the radiance of a foul soul showing through, and transfiguring, its clay container? The last, I think. For, O my poor old Harry Jekyll, if ever I read Satan’s signature on a face, it is on that of your new friend.”

Round the corner from the side street there was a square of ancient, handsome houses, now for the most part fallen from their high estate and let out in flats and chambers to all sorts and conditions of men: map-engravers, architects, shady lawyers and the agents of obscure enterprises. One house, however, the second from the corner, was still occupied entire. At the door of this house, which had a great air of wealth and comfort though it was now plunged in darkness except for the fanlight, Mr. Utterson stopped and knocked. A well-dressed, elderly servant opened the door.
“Is Dr. Jekyll at home, Poole?” asked the lawyer.

“I will find out, Mr. Utterson,” said Poole. He let the visitor into a large, low-roofed, comfortable hall paved with flagstones. It was warmed, like a country house, by a bright open fire, and furnished with costly oak cabinets. “Will you wait here by the fire, sir? Or shall I light you a lamp in the dining-room?”

“Here, thank you,” said the lawyer, and he went near and leaned on the tall fender. This hall, in which he was now left alone, was a pet fancy of his friend the doctor’s, and Utterson himself used to call it the pleasantest room in London. But tonight there was a shudder in his blood. The face of Hyde sat heavy on his memory. He felt—which was rare with him—a nausea and distaste for life, and in the gloom of his spirits he seemed to read a menace in the flickering of the firelight on the polished cabinets and the uneasy starting of the shadow on the ceiling. He was ashamed of his relief when Poole soon returned to announce that Dr. Jekyll had gone out.
“I saw Mr. Hyde go in through the old dissecting-room door, Poole,” he said. “Is that proper, with Dr. Jekyll away from home?”
“Quite right, Mr. Utterson, sir,” answered the servant. “Mr. Hyde has been given a key.”
“Your master seems to put a great deal of trust in that young man, Poole,” the other went on, musing.
“He does, sir, truly,” said Poole. “All of us have orders to do as he says.”
“I don’t think I have ever met Mr. Hyde?” asked Utterson.
“Oh, dear no, sir. He never _dines_ here,” answered the butler. “We see very little of him on this side of the house, to tell the truth. He mostly goes in and out through the laboratory.”
“Well, good night, Poole.”
“Good night, Mr. Utterson.”

And the lawyer set out for home with a very heavy heart. “Poor Harry Jekyll,” he thought. “I fear he is in deep waters! He was wild when he was young, a long while ago to be sure, but in the law of God there is no statute of limitations. Ah, it must be that: the ghost of some old sin, the cancer of some concealed disgrace. Punishment is coming, _pede claudo_, years after memory has forgotten the fault and self-love has excused it.” And the lawyer, scared by the thought, brooded a while on his own past, groping in all the corners of memory in case some Jack-in-the-Box of an old iniquity should leap to light there. His past was fairly blameless. Few men could read the rolls of their lives with less apprehension. Yet he was humbled to the dust by the many bad things he had done, and raised up again into a sober and fearful gratitude by the many he had come so near to doing and yet avoided. And then, returning to his former subject, he conceived a spark of hope. “This Master Hyde, if he were studied,” he thought, “must have secrets of his own—black secrets, by the look of him—secrets compared to which poor Jekyll’s worst would be like sunshine. Things cannot go on as they are. It turns me cold to think of this creature stealing like a thief to Harry’s bedside. Poor Harry, what a waking! And the danger of it, for if this Hyde suspects the existence of the will, he may grow impatient to inherit. Ah, I must put my shoulder to the wheel—if Jekyll will only let me,” he added. “If Jekyll will only let me.” For once more he saw before his mind’s eye, as clear as glass, the strange clauses of the will.

chapters.title: Dr. Jekyll Was Quite at Ease
paragraphs: A fortnight later, by excellent good fortune, the doctor gave one of his pleasant dinners to some five or six old friends, all intelligent, reputable men and all judges of good wine; and Mr. Utterson so arranged things that he stayed behind after the others had left. This was nothing new—it had happened dozens of times before. Where Utterson was liked, he was liked well. Hosts loved to keep the dry lawyer a while longer, once the light-hearted and loose-tongued already had their foot on the threshold; they liked to sit a bit in his unobtrusive company, practising for solitude, sobering their minds in the man’s rich silence after the expense and strain of gaiety. Dr. Jekyll was no exception to this rule; and as he now sat on the opposite side of the fire—a large, well-built, smooth-faced man of fifty, with something faintly sly about him perhaps, but every mark of ability and kindness—you could see by his expression that he felt a sincere and warm affection for Mr. Utterson.
“I’ve been wanting to speak to you, Jekyll,” Utterson began. “You know that will of yours?”

A close observer might have noticed that the subject was unwelcome; but the doctor carried it off lightly. “My poor Utterson,” he said, “you’re unlucky to have a client like me. I never saw a man so troubled as you were by my will—except perhaps that rigid pedant Lanyon, over what he called my scientific heresies. Oh, I know he’s a good fellow—you needn’t frown—an excellent fellow, and I always mean to see more of him; but a rigid pedant all the same; an ignorant, loud-mouthed pedant. I’ve never been more disappointed in any man than in Lanyon.”
“You know I never approved of it,” Utterson went on, refusing to be drawn onto the new subject.
“My will? Yes, of course I know that,” said the doctor, a little sharply. “You’ve told me so.”
“Well, I’m telling you again,” the lawyer continued. “I’ve been learning something about young Hyde.”
The large, handsome face of Dr. Jekyll went pale to the very lips, and a darkness came around his eyes. “I don’t care to hear any more,” he said. “This is a subject I thought we’d agreed to drop.”
“What I heard was appalling,” said Utterson.

“It can’t change anything. You don’t understand my position,” the doctor replied, with a certain unevenness in his manner. “I’m painfully placed, Utterson; my position is a very strange one—a very strange one indeed. It’s one of those situations that talking can’t mend.”
“Jekyll,” said Utterson, “you know me: I’m a man who can be trusted. Tell me the whole of it in confidence, and I have no doubt I can get you out of it.”

“My good Utterson,” said the doctor, “this is very good of you—downright good of you—and I can’t find words to thank you for it. I believe you completely; I’d trust you before any man alive, yes, before myself, if I could make the choice; but truly, it isn’t what you imagine; it isn’t as bad as that; and just to set your good heart at rest, I’ll tell you one thing: the moment I choose, I can be rid of Mr. Hyde. I give you my word on that; and I thank you again and again; and I’ll just add one more word, Utterson, that I’m sure you’ll take the right way: this is a private matter, and I beg you to let it rest.”
Utterson thought a little, looking into the fire.
“I’ve no doubt you’re perfectly right,” he said at last, rising to his feet.

“Well, but since we’ve touched on this business—and for the last time, I hope,” the doctor went on, “there’s one point I’d like you to understand. I really do take a great interest in poor Hyde. I know you’ve seen him; he told me so; and I’m afraid he was rude. But I do sincerely take a great, a very great interest in that young man; and if I’m taken away, Utterson, I want you to promise me that you’ll put up with him and see that he gets what’s due to him. I think you would, if you knew everything; and it would be a weight off my mind if you’d promise.”
“I can’t pretend I’ll ever like him,” said the lawyer.
“I’m not asking that,” Jekyll pleaded, laying his hand on the other’s arm. “I’m only asking for justice; I’m only asking you to help him for my sake, when I’m no longer here.”
Utterson let out a sigh he could not hold back. “Well,” he said, “I promise.”

chapters.title: The Carew Murder Case
paragraphs: Nearly a year later, in the month of October, 18—, London was shaken by a crime of singular ferocity, made all the more notable by the high standing of the victim. The details were few and startling. A maidservant living alone in a house not far from the river had gone up to bed around eleven. Though fog rolled over the city in the small hours, the early part of the night was cloudless, and the lane her window looked onto was lit brilliantly by the full moon. It seems she had a dreamy, fanciful streak, for she sat down on her trunk, which stood right under the window, and fell into a daydream. Never, she used to say afterwards, with tears streaming down her face as she told the story—never had she felt more at peace with everyone or thought more kindly of the world. And as she sat there, she noticed an aged, handsome, white-haired gentleman drawing near along the lane, and another gentleman, a very small one, advancing to meet him, to whom at first she paid little attention. When they came within speaking distance—right beneath the maid’s window—the older man bowed and greeted the other with a very charming show of politeness. It didn’t seem as if what he was saying was especially important; in fact, from the way he pointed, it sometimes looked as though he were only asking directions; but the moon shone on his face as he spoke, and the girl was pleased to watch it, for it seemed to breathe such an innocent, old-fashioned kindness of nature—yet with something lofty in it too, as of a man with good reason to be satisfied with himself. Presently her eye wandered to the other man, and she was surprised to recognise a certain Mr. Hyde, who had once visited her master and for whom she had taken a dislike. He had a heavy cane in his hand, which he was playing with idly; but he answered not a word, and seemed to listen with badly hidden impatience. And then all at once he broke into a great blaze of anger, stamping his foot, brandishing the cane, and carrying on—as the maid described it—like a madman. The old gentleman stepped back, looking very surprised and a little hurt; and at that Mr. Hyde flew past all restraint and clubbed him to the ground. And the next moment, with ape-like fury, he was trampling his victim underfoot and raining down a storm of blows, under which the bones could be heard breaking and the body jumped on the roadway. At the horror of these sights and sounds, the maid fainted.

It was two o’clock when she came to herself and called the police. The murderer was long gone by then; but his victim lay in the middle of the lane, mangled almost beyond belief. The stick with which the crime had been done, though it was made of some rare, tough, heavy wood, had snapped in two under the force of this senseless cruelty; and one splintered half had rolled into the gutter nearby—the other, no doubt, had been carried off by the murderer. A purse and a gold watch were found on the victim, but no cards or papers except a sealed and stamped envelope, which he had probably been carrying to the post, and which bore the name and address of Mr. Utterson.

This was brought to the lawyer the next morning before he was even out of bed; and no sooner had he seen it and been told the circumstances than he set his lips grimly. “I’ll say nothing until I’ve seen the body,” he said. “This may be very serious. Be good enough to wait while I dress.” And with the same grave face he hurried through breakfast and drove to the police station where the body had been taken. As soon as he entered the cell, he nodded.
“Yes,” he said, “I recognise him. I’m sorry to say this is Sir Danvers Carew.”

“Good God, sir,” exclaimed the officer, “is it possible?” And the next moment his eyes lit up with professional ambition. “This will make a great deal of noise,” he said. “And perhaps you can help us find the man.” And he briefly described what the maid had seen, and showed him the broken stick.

Mr. Utterson had already flinched at the name of Hyde; but when the stick was laid before him, he could doubt no longer—broken and battered as it was, he recognised it as one he had himself given, many years before, to Henry Jekyll.
“Is this Mr. Hyde a small man?” he asked.
“Particularly small and particularly wicked-looking, is what the maid calls him,” said the officer.
Mr. Utterson thought for a moment; then, raising his head, “If you’ll come with me in my cab,” he said, “I think I can take you to his house.”

It was by this time about nine in the morning, and the first fog of the season. A great chocolate-coloured pall hung low over the sky, but the wind kept charging and scattering these massed vapours, so that as the cab crawled from street to street, Mr. Utterson witnessed a remarkable range of shades and degrees of twilight; for here it would be dark as the end of evening, and there a glow of rich, lurid brown, like the light of some strange fire; and here, for a moment, the fog would break apart entirely and a ragged shaft of daylight would slip in between the swirling clouds. The dismal district of Soho, glimpsed through these shifting gaps, with its muddy streets, its shabby foot traffic, and its lamps, which had never been put out or had been relit to fight off this mournful return of darkness, seemed to the lawyer’s eyes like a district of some city in a nightmare. His thoughts, besides, were of the gloomiest sort; and when he glanced at his companion in the cab, he felt something of that dread of the law and its officers which can, at times, seize even the most honest of men.

As the cab pulled up at the address given, the fog lifted a little and showed him a dingy street, a gin shop, a cheap French eating house, a shop selling penny novels and twopenny salads, many ragged children huddled in doorways, and many women of many nationalities going out, key in hand, for a morning glass of drink; and the next moment the fog settled back down over that part of town, brown as umber, and cut him off from his disreputable surroundings. This was the home of Henry Jekyll’s favourite—a man who stood to inherit a quarter of a million pounds.

An ivory-faced, silver-haired old woman opened the door. She had a wicked face, smoothed over by hypocrisy, but her manners were excellent. Yes, she said, this was Mr. Hyde’s house, but he wasn’t in; he had come home very late that night, but had gone out again within the hour; there was nothing unusual in that, his habits were very irregular, and he was often away—for instance, it had been nearly two months since she’d seen him until yesterday.

“Very well, then, we want to see his rooms,” said the lawyer; and when the woman began protesting it was impossible, “I’d better tell you who this person is,” he added. “This is Inspector Newcomen of Scotland Yard.”
A flash of ugly delight crossed the woman’s face. “Ah!” she said, “he’s in trouble! What’s he done?”
Mr. Utterson and the inspector exchanged glances. “He don’t seem a very popular man,” the inspector observed. “Now then, my good woman, just let this gentleman and me have a look around.”

In the whole extent of the house, which apart from the old woman stood otherwise empty, Mr. Hyde had used only a couple of rooms; but these were furnished with luxury and good taste. A closet was stocked with wine; the tableware was silver, the linen elegant; a good painting hung on the wall, a gift, Utterson supposed, from Henry Jekyll, who was quite the connoisseur; and the carpets were thick-piled and pleasing in colour. At that moment, however, the rooms showed every sign of having been recently and hastily ransacked; clothes lay scattered on the floor with their pockets turned inside out; locked drawers stood open; and on the hearth lay a heap of grey ash, as though a great many papers had been burned. From these embers the inspector dug out the unburned stub of a green cheque book, which had survived the fire; the other half of the stick was found behind the door; and since this confirmed his suspicions, the officer declared himself delighted. A visit to the bank, where several thousand pounds were found lying to the murderer’s credit, completed his satisfaction.

“You may depend on it, sir,” he told Mr. Utterson: “I have him in my hand. He must have lost his head, or he’d never have left the stick, and above all never have burned the cheque book. Why, money’s life itself to a man like that. We’ve nothing to do but wait for him at the bank and put out the handbills.”

This last, however, wasn’t so easy to manage; for Mr. Hyde had had few close acquaintances—even the maid’s employer had seen him only twice; his family could nowhere be traced; he had never been photographed; and the few who could describe him disagreed widely, as ordinary witnesses will. On only one point were they in agreement: the haunting sense of some indescribable deformity that the fugitive left with everyone who saw him.

chapters.title: Incident of the Letter
paragraphs: Late that afternoon Mr. Utterson called at Dr. Jekyll’s door, where Poole let him in at once. The butler took him through the kitchen quarters and over a yard that had once been a garden, to the building people called, without much distinction, the laboratory or the dissecting-rooms. The doctor had bought the house from the heirs of a famous surgeon. Since his own tastes were chemical rather than anatomical, he had put the block at the bottom of the garden to a different use. The lawyer had never before been admitted to this part of his friend’s premises. He studied the dingy, windowless building with curiosity, and as he crossed the theatre he felt an uneasy strangeness all around him. Eager students had once packed the place; now it lay gaunt and silent. The tables were loaded with chemical apparatus, crates stood about, packing straw littered the floor, and a dim light came down through the foggy dome. At the far end, a flight of stairs rose to a door covered in red baize, and through it Mr. Utterson was at last shown into the doctor’s study. It was a large room, lined with glass cupboards and furnished, among other things, with a full-length mirror and a business table. Three dusty, iron-barred windows looked out on the court. A fire was burning in the grate, and a lit lamp stood on the mantelpiece, since the fog was already thickening even inside the houses. Close up to the warmth sat Dr. Jekyll, looking deathly sick. He did not rise to greet his visitor. He held out a cold hand instead, and bade him welcome in a voice that had changed.
“Well,” said Mr. Utterson, the moment Poole had left them, “you have heard the news?”
The doctor shuddered. “Newsboys were calling it out in the square,” he said. “I could hear them in my dining-room.”
“Let me ask one thing,” said the lawyer. “Carew was my client, and so are you, and I need to know what I am doing. Tell me you haven’t been mad enough to hide this fellow.”

“Utterson, I swear to God,” cried the doctor, “I swear to God that I will never set eyes on him again. I give you my word of honour that I have finished with him in this world. It is all at an end. And in truth he doesn’t want my help. You don’t know him as I do. He is safe, perfectly safe. Mark my words: nobody will ever hear of him again.”

The lawyer listened with a heavy heart, for he disliked his friend’s feverish manner. “You seem very certain of him,” he said, “and for your sake I hope you’re right. If there were a trial, your name might be brought into it.”

“I am quite certain of him,” replied Jekyll. “My reasons for it are ones I can’t share with anyone. But there is one matter on which you can advise me. I have—I have had a letter, and I can’t decide whether to show it to the police. I would like to put it in your hands, Utterson. You would judge it wisely, I’m sure. I trust you absolutely.”
“I take it you’re afraid it might help them find him?” asked the lawyer.
“No,” said the other. “I can’t claim to care what happens to Hyde. I have finished with him altogether. It was my own good name I was thinking of, which this hateful affair has left rather exposed.”
Utterson brooded over this for some time. His friend’s selfishness surprised him, yet it also came as a relief. “Well,” he said at last, “let me see the letter.”

The letter was in an odd, upright hand, and signed “Edward Hyde.” In short, it told Dr. Jekyll, his benefactor, whom the writer had for so long repaid so unworthily for a thousand kindnesses, that he need have no fear for the writer’s safety, because he had a way of escape that he could count on. The lawyer thought quite well of this letter. It cast the acquaintance in a better light than he had expected, and he reproached himself for some of his earlier suspicions.
“Have you got the envelope?” he asked.
“I burned it,” replied Jekyll, “before I had thought what I was doing. But there was no postmark on it. The note was brought by hand.”
“Shall I hold on to this and sleep on it?” asked Utterson.
“I want you to decide for me entirely,” was the reply. “I no longer trust my own judgement.”
“Very well, I shall consider it,” returned the lawyer. “And now one more question. Was it Hyde who dictated the wording in your will about your disappearance?”
The doctor looked as if a faintness had come over him. He pressed his lips together and nodded.
“I knew it,” said Utterson. “He meant to murder you. You have had a fine escape.”
“I have had something far more useful than that,” the doctor answered solemnly. “I have had a lesson—O God, Utterson, what a lesson I have had!” And for a moment he hid his face in his hands.

As he left, the lawyer paused to exchange a word or two with Poole. “By the way,” he said, “someone brought a letter by hand today. What was the messenger like?” But Poole was certain that nothing had arrived except by post, “and only circulars even then,” he added.

This news sent the visitor away with his fears renewed. Plainly the letter had come in through the laboratory door. It might even have been written in the study itself, and in that case it had to be weighed differently and handled with greater care. As he walked, newsboys were shouting themselves hoarse along the pavements: “Special edition. Shocking murder of an M.P.” That was the funeral oration for one friend and client, and he could not help dreading that the good name of another might be dragged down in the whirlpool of the scandal. The choice before him was at the least a delicate one. Self-reliant though he was by habit, he began to long for advice. He could not ask for it outright, but perhaps, he thought, he could angle for it.

Before long he was seated on one side of his own hearth, with Mr. Guest, his head clerk, facing him on the other. Between them, at a carefully measured distance from the fire, stood a bottle of a particular old wine that had lain long unsunned in the foundations of his house. Fog still slept on the wing above the drowned city, where the lamps shone like carbuncles, and through the muffling and smothering of those fallen clouds the life of the town went on streaming along its great arteries with a sound like a mighty wind. But the room was cheerful with firelight. In the bottle the acids had long since settled. The imperial purple had mellowed with age, as colour deepens in stained glass, and the glow of hot autumn afternoons on hillside vineyards was ready to be released and to drive off the fogs of London. Unawares, the lawyer softened. There was no man from whom he kept fewer secrets than Mr. Guest, and he was not always sure that he kept as many as he intended. Guest had often called on the doctor on business, and knew Poole. He could scarcely have missed hearing that Mr. Hyde came and went freely in the house, and he might draw his own conclusions. Would it not be as well, then, to let him see a letter that settled that mystery? Above all, Guest was a keen student and critic of handwriting, and would find the step natural and obliging. Besides, the clerk was a man of sound counsel. He could hardly read so strange a document without letting fall some remark, and from that remark Mr. Utterson might decide what course to take.
“It’s a sad business, this about Sir Danvers,” he said.
“Yes, sir, indeed. It has aroused a great deal of public feeling,” returned Guest. “The man, of course, was mad.”

“I would like to hear what you make of that,” replied Utterson. “I have a paper here in his handwriting. Keep it between ourselves, because I hardly know what to do with it. It is an ugly business at the best of times. But there it is, and just in your line: a murderer’s autograph.”
Guest’s eyes lit up. He sat down at once and pored over it with zest. “No, sir,” he said, “not mad. But it is an odd hand.”
“And by every account a very odd man to write it,” added the lawyer.
At that moment the servant came in with a note.
“Is that from Dr. Jekyll, sir?” the clerk asked. “I thought I recognised the writing. Is it anything private, Mr. Utterson?”
“Only an invitation to dinner. Why? Would you like to see it?”

“Just for a moment. Thank you, sir.” The clerk laid the two sheets of paper side by side and went carefully over what was written on them. “Thank you, sir,” he said finally, handing them both back. “It’s a most interesting autograph.”
A pause followed, in which Mr. Utterson fought with himself. “Why did you compare them, Guest?” he asked suddenly.
“Well, sir,” the clerk answered, “there’s a rather curious likeness. The two hands match in many points. Only the slope is different.”
“Rather odd,” said Utterson.
“It is, as you say, rather odd,” returned Guest.
“I shouldn’t speak of this note, you understand,” said his employer.
“No, sir,” said the clerk. “I understand.”

But as soon as Mr. Utterson was alone that night, he locked the note away in his safe, and there it stayed from then on. “What!” he thought. “Henry Jekyll, forging a letter for a murderer!” And his blood ran cold.

chapters.title: Remarkable Incident of Doctor Lanyon
paragraphs: Time went by; a reward of thousands of pounds was offered, since the public felt Sir Danvers’s death as an injury to itself; but Mr. Hyde had vanished from the knowledge of the police as though he had never existed. A great deal of his past was dug up, and none of it was to his credit: stories emerged of the man’s cruelty—as callous as it was violent—of his vile life, his strange companions, and the hatred that seemed to have dogged his whole career; but as to where he now was, not a word. From the moment he left the house in Soho on the morning of the murder, he was simply erased; and gradually, as time passed, Mr. Utterson began to recover from the height of his alarm and to grow easier in his mind. To his way of thinking, the death of Sir Danvers was more than paid for by Mr. Hyde’s disappearance. Now that this evil influence had been lifted, a new life began for Dr. Jekyll. He came out of his seclusion, renewed his old friendships, once again became their familiar guest and host; and while he had always been known for his charitable works, he was now no less noted for his religious observance. He kept busy, spent much time outdoors, did good works; his face seemed to open and brighten, as though with an inward sense of service performed; and for more than two months the doctor knew peace.

On the 8th of January Utterson had dined at the doctor’s house with a small party; Lanyon had been there too; and their host’s face had turned from one to the other just as in the old days when the three of them had been inseparable. On the 12th, and again on the 14th, the door was shut against the lawyer. “The doctor is confined to the house,” Poole told him, “and sees no one.” On the 15th he tried once more and was again turned away; and having grown used, over the past two months, to seeing his friend nearly every day, he found this return to solitude weighing on his spirits. On the fifth night he had Guest in to dine with him; on the sixth he made his way to Dr. Lanyon’s.

There at least he was not refused admittance; but once inside, he was shocked at the change that had come over the doctor’s appearance. His face had his death sentence written on it plainly. The once ruddy man had grown pale; his flesh had wasted away; he was visibly balder and older; and yet it was not so much these marks of a swift physical decline that caught the lawyer’s attention as something in his eye and manner that seemed to speak of some deep terror in his mind. It seemed unlikely that the doctor should fear death; yet that was exactly what Utterson found himself suspecting. “Yes,” he thought; “he is a doctor, he must know his own condition and that his days are numbered; and the knowledge is more than he can bear.” And yet when Utterson remarked on how ill he looked, it was with an air of great resolve that Lanyon declared himself a doomed man.

“I have had a shock,” he said, “and I shall never recover from it. It’s a matter of weeks now. Well, life has been pleasant; I liked it; yes, sir, I used to like it. I sometimes think that if we knew everything, we should be gladder to get away.”
“Jekyll is ill too,” Utterson observed. “Have you seen him?”

But Lanyon’s face changed, and he raised a trembling hand. “I want to see or hear no more of Dr. Jekyll,” he said, in a loud, unsteady voice. “I am quite done with that person, and I beg you to spare me any mention of someone I now regard as dead.”
“Tut, tut,” said Mr. Utterson; then, after a considerable pause, “Can’t I do anything?” he asked. “We are three very old friends, Lanyon; we shall not live to make others.”
“Nothing can be done,” Lanyon answered. “Ask him yourself.”
“He will not see me,” said the lawyer.

“I am not surprised at that,” came the reply. “Someday, Utterson, after I am dead, you may perhaps come to learn the right and wrong of this. I cannot tell you now. And in the meantime, if you can sit and talk with me of other things, then for God’s sake stay and do so; but if you cannot keep off this accursed subject, then in God’s name go, for I cannot bear it.”

As soon as he got home, Utterson sat down and wrote to Jekyll, complaining of being shut out of the house and asking the cause of this unhappy break with Lanyon; the next day brought a long reply, worded in places quite movingly, and elsewhere darkly obscure in its meaning. The quarrel with Lanyon was beyond mending. “I do not blame our old friend,” Jekyll wrote, “but I share his view that we must never meet again. From now on I mean to live in the strictest seclusion; you must not be surprised, nor doubt my friendship for you, if my door is often shut even to you. You must let me go my own dark way. I have brought upon myself a punishment and a danger I cannot name. If I am the chief of sinners, I am the chief of sufferers also. I could not have believed this earth held room for suffering and terror so unmanning as this; and there is only one thing you can do, Utterson, to lighten this fate of mine, and that is to respect my silence.” Utterson was amazed; with Hyde’s dark influence withdrawn, the doctor had gone back to his old work and old friendships; only a week before, the outlook had promised a cheerful and honoured old age; and now, in a moment, friendship, peace of mind, the entire course of his life lay wrecked. So great and unlooked-for a change suggested madness; but given Lanyon’s manner and words, there had to be some deeper cause.

A week later Dr. Lanyon took to his bed, and in under a fortnight he was dead. The night after the funeral, at which he had been deeply moved, Utterson locked the door of his office and, sitting there by the light of a single melancholy candle, drew out and set before him an envelope addressed in the hand and sealed with the seal of his dead friend. “PRIVATE: for the hands of G. J. Utterson ALONE, and should he die first, to be destroyed unread”—so it was pointedly marked; and the lawyer dreaded to look at what was inside. “I have buried one friend today,” he thought: “what if this should cost me another?” Then he condemned the fear as disloyal and broke the seal. Inside was a second, sealed enclosure, marked on the cover “not to be opened till the death or disappearance of Dr. Henry Jekyll.” Utterson could hardly believe his eyes. Yes, it said disappearance; here again, just as in the mad will he had long ago returned to its author, here again were the notion of a disappearance and the name of Henry Jekyll linked together. But in the will, that notion had sprung from the sinister suggestion of the man Hyde; it had been set there with a purpose all too plain and horrible. Written in Lanyon’s own hand, what could it mean? A great curiosity seized the trustee, to disregard the prohibition and dive straight to the bottom of these mysteries; but professional honour and loyalty to his dead friend were binding obligations, and the packet went to sleep in the innermost corner of his private safe.

It is one thing to hold curiosity in check, another to conquer it altogether; and it may be doubted whether, from that day on, Utterson wished for his surviving friend’s company with quite the same eagerness. He thought of him with kindness, but his thoughts were troubled and fearful. He did go to call; but he was perhaps relieved to be turned away; perhaps, in his heart, he preferred to speak with Poole on the doorstep, surrounded by the air and sounds of the open city, rather than be admitted into that house of voluntary imprisonment and sit talking with its unreadable recluse. Poole, in fact, had no very pleasant news to give him. The doctor, it appeared, now confined himself more than ever to the study above the laboratory, where he sometimes even slept; he was low in spirits, had grown very silent, did not read; it seemed as though something weighed on his mind. Utterson grew so used to the unchanging character of these reports that he gradually visited less and less often.

chapters.title: Incident at the Window
paragraphs: One Sunday, as Mr. Utterson was taking his usual walk with Mr. Enfield, they happened to pass once more along the by-street. Opposite the door they both halted and stared at it.
“Well,” said Enfield, “at any rate, that story has ended. We shan’t see any more of Mr. Hyde.”
“I hope not,” said Utterson. “Have I ever told you that I met him once myself, and felt the same revulsion you did?”

“You couldn’t feel the one without the other,” Enfield answered. “And by the way, you must have taken me for a perfect ass, not to see that this was a back entrance to Dr. Jekyll’s! Even when I did find out, it was partly your doing.”

“So you did find out, then?” said Utterson. “If so, we can go into the court and have a look up at the windows. To be honest, I’m uneasy about poor Jekyll. Even from outside, I feel that a friend’s being near might do him some good.”

It was very cool in the court, and a little damp, and already filled with twilight, though high above the sky still glowed with the sunset. The middle window of the three was open halfway. Beside it, and sitting very close, breathing the air with an endless sadness in his face, like some forlorn prisoner, Utterson saw Dr. Jekyll.
“What! Jekyll! Jekyll!” he called. “I hope you’re better.”
“I’m very low, Utterson,” the doctor answered wearily, “very low. It won’t last long, thank God.”

“You spend too much time indoors,” said the lawyer. “You ought to be out walking and setting your blood moving, as Mr. Enfield and I are. (This is my cousin—Mr. Enfield—Dr. Jekyll.) Come along now, get your hat and take a short turn with us.”

“That’s kind of you,” the other sighed. “I would like to very much. But no, no, no, it’s quite out of the question. I daren’t. Still, Utterson, I’m truly glad to see you. It’s a real pleasure. I would ask you and Mr. Enfield to come up, but the room is not fit to receive anyone.”
“Why, then,” said the lawyer good-humouredly, “the best thing is for us to stay down here and talk to you where we stand.”

“I was just going to make that very suggestion,” answered the doctor with a smile. But hardly had he said it when the smile vanished from his face, and in its place came a look of such abject terror and despair that the two gentlemen below felt their blood turn to ice. They caught only a glimpse, because the window was slammed shut at once. But a glimpse was enough, and they turned and left the court without speaking. They went back along the by-street in silence as well. Only when they had reached a nearby thoroughfare, where even on a Sunday some life still stirred, did Mr. Utterson turn at last and look at his companion. Both were pale, and the same horror looked back at him from Enfield’s eyes.
“God forgive us, God forgive us,” said Mr. Utterson.
Mr. Enfield only nodded, with great gravity, and walked on again without a word.

chapters.title: The Last Night
paragraphs: One evening, as Mr. Utterson sat by his fire after dinner, he was surprised by a visit from Poole.
“Bless me, Poole, what brings you here?” he cried. Then, looking at him a second time, he added, “What ails you? Is the doctor ill?”
“Mr. Utterson,” said the man, “something is wrong.”
“Sit down, and have a glass of wine,” said the lawyer. “Now, take your time, and tell me plainly what you’ve come for.”

“You know the doctor’s ways, sir,” replied Poole, “and how he shuts himself away. Well, he’s shut himself up in the study again. And I don’t like it, sir—I wish I may die if I do. Mr. Utterson, sir, I’m afraid.”
“Come now, my good man,” said the lawyer, “say it clearly. What are you afraid of?”
“I’ve been afraid for about a week,” said Poole, stubbornly paying no attention to the question, “and I can’t stand it any longer.”

The man’s looks bore out every word. He had changed for the worse. Apart from the moment when he first spoke of his terror, he had not once met the lawyer’s eye. Even now he sat with the wine untasted on his knee, staring at a corner of the floor. “I can’t stand it any longer,” he said again.
“Come,” said the lawyer, “I see you have good reason, Poole. I see that something is seriously amiss. Try to tell me what.”
“I think there’s been foul play,” Poole said hoarsely.
“Foul play!” cried the lawyer, who was a good deal alarmed and, in consequence, rather inclined to be irritable. “What foul play! What does the man mean?”
“I daren’t say, sir,” was the answer. “But will you come with me and see it for yourself?”

Mr. Utterson answered only by getting up and taking his hat and greatcoat. He noticed with wonder how deeply relieved the butler looked, and with perhaps equal wonder that the wine was still untouched when Poole set the glass down to follow him.

It was a wild, cold March night, the kind the season brings, with a pale moon lying on her back as if the wind had tipped her over, and torn cloud streaming past, as fine as gauze. The wind made talking hard and stung the blood into their faces. It seemed, too, to have swept the streets unusually bare of passers-by, for Mr. Utterson felt he had never seen that part of London so empty. He would have liked it otherwise. Never in his life had he felt so keen a longing to see and touch other human beings. However hard he fought it, a crushing sense that disaster was coming kept pressing on his mind. By the time they reached the square it was full of wind and dust, and the thin trees in the garden were whipping themselves against the railing. Poole, who had stayed a pace or two ahead all the way, now halted in the middle of the pavement. Despite the bitter weather he took off his hat and wiped his forehead with a red handkerchief. Yet for all his haste in coming, it was not the sweat of exertion that he wiped away. It was the damp of some choking anguish, for his face was white, and his voice, when he spoke, was harsh and broken.
“Well, sir,” he said, “here we are, and God grant nothing is wrong.”
“Amen, Poole,” said the lawyer.
Then the servant gave a very cautious knock. The door was opened on its chain, and a voice from inside asked, “Is that you, Poole?”
“It’s all right,” said Poole. “Open up.”

When they entered, the hall was brightly lit and the fire piled high. Around the hearth the whole household, men and women alike, stood huddled together like a flock of sheep. When she saw Mr. Utterson, the housemaid burst into hysterical whimpering, and the cook cried out, “Thank God! It’s Mr. Utterson,” and rushed forward as though to take him in her arms.
“What is this? Are you all here?” the lawyer said crossly. “This is most irregular and most unseemly. Your master would be far from pleased.”
“They’re all frightened,” said Poole.
No one protested, and a blank silence followed. Only the maid raised her voice, and now she wept aloud.

“Be quiet!” Poole told her, with a savagery in his tone that showed how frayed his own nerves were. Indeed, when the girl had suddenly lifted her lament, they had all started and turned to the inner door with faces full of dreadful expectation. “And now,” the butler went on, turning to the knife-boy, “give me a candle, and we’ll get this settled at once.” Then he asked Mr. Utterson to come with him, and led the way into the back garden.
“Now, sir,” he said, “come as softly as you can. I want you to listen, but I don’t want you to be heard. And look here, sir, if by any chance he asks you to come in, don’t go.”

This unexpected warning gave Mr. Utterson’s nerves such a jolt that he nearly lost his footing. But he steadied his courage and followed the butler into the laboratory building, across the surgical theatre with its jumble of crates and bottles, to the foot of the stairs. There Poole signed to him to stand aside and listen. He himself put down the candle, plainly forcing up all his resolve, climbed the steps and rapped with a rather unsteady hand on the red baize of the study door.
“Mr. Utterson, sir, has come to see you,” he called. And even as he said it, he gestured fiercely once more for the lawyer to listen.
A voice answered from inside: “Tell him I can’t see anyone,” it said fretfully.

“Thank you, sir,” said Poole, with something like triumph in his voice. He picked up his candle and led Mr. Utterson back across the yard to the great kitchen, where the fire was out and beetles were hopping about on the floor.
“Sir,” he said, looking Mr. Utterson in the eye, “was that my master’s voice?”
“It seems very much altered,” replied the lawyer, very pale, but meeting his gaze.

“Altered? Well, yes, I think so,” said the butler. “Twenty years I’ve been in this man’s house. Do you think I’d be fooled about his voice? No, sir. My master has been made away with. He was made away with eight days ago, when we heard him cry out the name of God. And _who’s_ in there in his place, and _why_ it stays there, is a thing that cries out to Heaven, Mr. Utterson!”

“This is a very strange tale, Poole. It’s a rather wild one, my man,” said Mr. Utterson, biting his finger. “Suppose it were as you think, and Dr. Jekyll had been—well, murdered. What could make the murderer stay? That won’t hold water. Reason won’t support it.”

“Well, Mr. Utterson, you’re a hard man to satisfy, but I’ll manage it yet,” said Poole. “All this last week (you must understand) him, or it, whatever it is that lives in that study, has been crying night and day for some sort of medicine, and can’t get it right. It was sometimes his way—the master’s, I mean—to write his orders on a sheet of paper and throw it down the stairs. That’s all we’ve had this past week: papers, and a shut door, and the very meals left outside to be smuggled in when no one was looking. Well, sir, every day, yes, and two and three times a day, there have been orders and complaints, and I’ve been sent running to every wholesale chemist in town. Each time I brought the stuff back, there’d be another paper telling me to return it, because it wasn’t pure, and another order to a different firm. Whatever it’s for, sir, this drug is wanted terribly.”
“Have you any of these papers?” asked Mr. Utterson.

Poole fumbled in his pocket and brought out a crumpled note. The lawyer bent toward the candle and went through it with care. It ran like this: “Dr. Jekyll presents his compliments to Messrs. Maw. He assures them that their last sample is impure and quite useless for his present purpose. In the year 18—, Dr. J. bought a rather large quantity from Messrs. M. He now begs them to search with the utmost care, and if any of the same quality is left, to forward it to him at once. Expense is no consideration. The importance of this to Dr. J. can hardly be overstated.” So far the letter had gone on calmly enough, but here, with a sudden splutter of the pen, the writer’s feelings had broken loose. “For God’s sake,” he had added, “find me some of the old.”
“This is a strange note,” said Mr. Utterson. Then, sharply: “How is it that you have it open?”
“The man at Maw’s was fearfully angry, sir, and threw it back at me like dirt,” Poole replied.
“There is no doubt that this is the doctor’s handwriting. Did you know that?” the lawyer pressed on.
“I thought it looked like it,” said the servant, rather sullenly. Then, in another tone: “But what does handwriting matter?” he said. “I’ve seen him!”
“Seen him?” repeated Mr. Utterson. “Well?”

“That’s it!” said Poole. “It happened like this. I walked into the theatre from the garden, unexpected. It seems he’d slipped out to look for this drug, or whatever it is, because the study door was open, and there he was at the far end of the room, digging through the crates. He looked up as I came in, let out a kind of cry, and bolted upstairs into the study. I saw him for no more than a minute, but the hair stood on end on my head like quills. Sir, if that was my master, why was there a mask on his face? If it was my master, why did he squeal like a rat and run from me? I’ve served him long enough. And then…” The man stopped and passed his hand over his face.

“These are all very strange circumstances,” said Mr. Utterson, “but I think I’m beginning to see daylight. Poole, your master has plainly been seized by one of those illnesses that torture the sufferer and disfigure him as well. That would account, for all I know, for the change in his voice. It would account for the mask, and for his keeping away from his friends, and for his eagerness to find this drug, by which the poor soul still hopes to be cured in the end—God grant he isn’t deceived! That is my explanation. It is sad enough, Poole, yes, and dreadful to think of, but it is plain and natural, it holds together well, and it spares us any extravagant alarms.”

“Sir,” said the butler, going a sort of blotchy white, “that thing was not my master, and that’s the truth. My master”—here he glanced around and began to whisper—“is a tall, well-built man, and this was more of a dwarf.” Utterson tried to object. “O, sir,” cried Poole, “do you think I don’t know my own master after twenty years? Do you think I don’t know where his head reaches in the study doorway, where I saw him every morning of my life? No, sir, that masked thing was never Dr. Jekyll. God knows what it was, but it was never Dr. Jekyll. And in my heart I believe that murder was done.”

“Poole,” answered the lawyer, “if that is what you say, I am bound to make sure. I want very much to spare your master’s feelings, and this note, which seems to prove that he is still alive, puzzles me. But I shall think it my duty to break down that door.”
“Ah, Mr. Utterson, now that’s talking!” cried the butler.
“And now comes the second question,” Utterson continued. “Who is to do it?”
“Why, you and me, sir,” came the fearless answer.
“Well said,” returned the lawyer, “and whatever happens, I’ll see to it that you lose nothing by it.”
“There’s an axe in the theatre,” Poole went on, “and you can take the kitchen poker for yourself.”
The lawyer took that rough but heavy tool in his hand and weighed it. “Do you realise, Poole,” he said, glancing up, “that you and I are about to put ourselves in some peril?”
“You may well say so, sir, indeed,” answered the butler.
“Then we had better be frank,” said the other. “We each think more than we’ve said, so let us hold nothing back. This masked figure you saw—did you recognise it?”

“Well, sir, it went so fast, and the creature was so hunched over, that I could hardly swear to it,” was the answer. “But if you’re asking whether it was Mr. Hyde, why, yes, I think it was! It was much the same size, you see, and it had the same quick, light way of moving. And who else could have got in by the laboratory door? You haven’t forgotten, sir, that when the murder happened he still had the key with him? But that’s not all. I don’t know, Mr. Utterson, whether you ever met this Mr. Hyde?”
“Yes,” said the lawyer, “I once talked with him.”

“Then you must know, like all the rest of us, that there was something queer about that gentleman—something that made a man shudder. I don’t rightly know how to put it, sir, except that you felt it in your marrow, cold and thin somehow.”
“I admit I felt something like what you describe,” said Mr. Utterson.

“Just so, sir,” Poole replied. “Well, when that masked thing, like a monkey, leapt up from among the chemicals and darted into the study, it ran down my spine like ice. O, I know it isn’t proof, Mr. Utterson. I’ve enough book-learning to know that. But a man has his feelings, and on my Bible oath, it was Mr. Hyde!”

“Yes, yes,” said the lawyer. “My own fears lead the same way. Evil, I fear, was bound to come out of that connection. Yes, indeed, I believe you. I believe poor Harry has been killed, and I believe his murderer (for what purpose, only God can tell) is still lurking in his victim’s room. Well, let vengeance be our watchword. Call Bradshaw.”
The footman answered the summons, very white and nervous.

“Pull yourself together, Bradshaw,” said the lawyer. “I know this suspense is wearing on all of you, but now we mean to finish it. Poole and I are going to break into the study. If all is well, my shoulders are broad enough to take the blame. In the meantime, in case something really is wrong, or some villain tries to get away by the back, you and the boy must go round the corner with a couple of good sticks and stand guard at the laboratory door. We’ll give you ten minutes to get into position.”

As Bradshaw went out, the lawyer looked at his watch. “And now, Poole, let’s take up ours,” he said. He tucked the poker under his arm and led the way into the yard. Racing cloud had banked over the moon, and it was now quite dark. The wind blew only in gusts and eddies into that deep well of buildings, and tossed the candle’s light about their feet until they reached the shelter of the theatre, where they sat down in silence to wait. London droned solemnly all around. Close at hand, however, the stillness was broken only by the sound of footsteps pacing back and forth across the study floor.

“It’ll walk like that all day, sir,” Poole whispered, “yes, and most of the night. It only pauses a little when a new sample comes from the chemist. Ah, a bad conscience is a great enemy of rest! Ah, sir, there’s blood foully shed in every step of it! But listen again, a little closer—put your heart into your ears, Mr. Utterson, and tell me, is that the doctor’s step?”

The footsteps fell lightly and strangely, with a kind of sway, though they were so slow. They were quite unlike Henry Jekyll’s heavy, creaking tread. Utterson sighed. “Is there never anything else?” he asked.
Poole nodded. “Once,” he said. “Once I heard it weeping!”
“Weeping? How so?” said the lawyer, feeling a sudden chill of horror.
“Weeping like a woman, or a soul in torment,” said the butler. “I went away with such a weight on my heart that I could have wept myself.”

But now the ten minutes were nearly over. Poole pulled the axe out from under a pile of packing straw. The candle was put on the nearest table to light their attack, and holding their breath they approached the spot where that patient step was still going up and down, up and down, in the quiet of the night.

“Jekyll,” Utterson called loudly, “I demand to see you.” He paused for a moment, but no answer came. “I warn you fairly: our suspicions are aroused, and I must and will see you,” he continued. “If not by fair means, then by foul—if not with your consent, then by brute force!”
“Utterson,” said the voice, “for God’s sake, have mercy!”
“Ah, that isn’t Jekyll’s voice. It’s Hyde’s!” cried Utterson. “Down with the door, Poole!”

Poole swung the axe up over his shoulder. The blow shook the building, and the red baize door jumped against its lock and hinges. A dismal shriek, of pure animal terror, rang out from the study. The axe rose again, and again the panels cracked and the frame leapt. Four times the blow came down, but the wood was hard and the fittings were superbly made, and only at the fifth stroke did the lock burst and the wreck of the door fall inward onto the carpet.

The besiegers, appalled by their own uproar and by the silence that followed it, drew back a little and looked in. The study lay before them in the quiet lamplight. A good fire glowed and crackled on the hearth, the kettle sang its thin song, a drawer or two stood open, papers were set out neatly on the business table, and nearer the fire the tea things were laid. It was the quietest room you could imagine, and, apart from the glass cupboards full of chemicals, the most ordinary in London that night.

Right in the middle lay a man’s body, horribly twisted and still twitching. They crept up on tiptoe, rolled it onto its back, and saw the face of Edward Hyde. He wore clothes much too big for him, clothes cut to the doctor’s size. The sinews of his face still moved as if with life, but life was quite gone. From the crushed phial in his hand and the strong smell of kernels in the air, Utterson knew he was looking at the body of a man who had taken his own life.
“We have come too late,” he said sternly, “whether to save him or to punish him. Hyde has gone to his reckoning, and all that remains is for us to find your master’s body.”

The theatre took up by far the greater part of the building. It filled almost the entire ground floor and was lit from above. The study formed an upper floor at one end and looked onto the court. A corridor joined the theatre to the door in the by-street, and the study had its own connection to this by a second flight of stairs. There were also a few dark closets and a roomy cellar. They now searched all of these thoroughly. Each closet needed only a glance, for all were empty, and the dust that fell from their doors showed they had long been left shut. The cellar, it is true, was crammed with rickety lumber, most of it from the days of the surgeon who had lived there before Jekyll. But as they opened the door they were warned that more searching was pointless, because a thick mat of cobweb, which had sealed the entrance for years, fell away. Nowhere was there any sign of Henry Jekyll, dead or alive.
Poole stamped on the flagstones of the corridor. “He must be buried here,” he said, listening to the sound.
“Or he may have run away,” said Utterson, and he turned to examine the door on the by-street. It was locked, and on the flagstones close by they found the key, already stained with rust.
“That doesn’t look as if it’s been used,” the lawyer remarked.
